paragraphs: The room where retired captain Snegiryov’s family lived is already familiar to the reader. At that moment it was stuffy and crowded with visitors. Several boys were sitting with Ilusha. Like Smurov, all of them were ready to deny that it was Alyosha who had brought them and made peace between them and Ilusha, but that was the truth. All his craft had consisted in taking them to Ilusha one at a time, without any “sheepish sentimentality,” and making it look casual and unplanned. It was a great comfort to Ilusha in his suffering. He was deeply touched to see the almost tender affection and sympathy of these boys, who had once been his enemies. Only Krassotkin was missing, and his absence weighed heavily on Ilusha’s heart. Perhaps the bitterest of all his bitter memories was that he had stabbed Krassotkin, his one friend and protector. Clever little Smurov, who was the first to make up with Ilusha, thought so too. But when Smurov hinted to Krassotkin that Alyosha wanted to come and see him about something, Krassotkin cut him short. He told Smurov to tell “Karamazov” right away that he knew best what to do, that he wanted no one’s advice, and that if he went to see Ilusha he would choose his own time, because he had “his own reasons.”

That was two weeks before this Sunday. That was why Alyosha had not been to see him, as he had meant to. But he waited, and he sent Smurov to Krassotkin twice more. Both times Krassotkin met him with a curt, impatient refusal. He sent Alyosha word not to pester him any more, and said that if Alyosha came himself, he, Krassotkin, would not go to Ilusha at all. Right up to the last day Smurov did not know that Kolya meant to go to Ilusha that morning. Only the evening before, as they parted, Kolya abruptly told him to wait at home for him next morning, because he would go with him to the Snegiryovs’. But he warned him not to say a word about his coming, since he wanted to drop in casually. Smurov obeyed. Smurov’s hunch that Kolya would bring back the lost dog rested on something Kolya had let drop, that “they must be asses not to find the dog, if it was alive.” When Smurov, waiting for a chance, timidly hinted at his guess about the dog, Krassotkin flew into a violent rage. “I’m not such an ass as to go hunting about the town for other people’s dogs when I’ve got a dog of my own! And how can you imagine a dog could be alive after swallowing a pin? Sheepish sentimentality, that’s what it is!”

For the last two weeks Ilusha had not left his little bed under the icons in the corner. He had not been to school since the day he met Alyosha and bit his finger. He had fallen ill the same day, though for a month afterwards he was sometimes able to get up and walk about the room and the passage. Lately, though, he had grown so weak that he could not move without his father’s help. His father was terribly worried about him. He had even given up drinking and was almost crazy with fear that his boy would die. Often, especially after walking Ilusha around the room on his arm and putting him back to bed, he would run to a dark corner of the passage, lean his head against the wall and break into violent fits of weeping, stifling his sobs so that Ilusha would not hear them.

When he came back into the room, he would usually start doing something to amuse and comfort his precious boy. He would tell him stories and funny anecdotes, or mimic comical people he had happened to meet, or even imitate the howls and cries of animals. But Ilusha could not bear to see his father fooling around and playing the buffoon. The boy tried not to show how much he disliked it, but he saw with an aching heart that his father was an object of contempt. He was haunted all the time by the memory of the “wisp of tow” and that “terrible day.”

Nina, Ilusha’s gentle, crippled sister, did not like her father’s buffoonery either (Varvara had gone off some time ago to study at the university in Petersburg). But the half-witted mother was greatly entertained and laughed heartily when her husband began capering about or acting something out. It was the only way she could be amused. The rest of the time she grumbled and complained that everyone had forgotten her now, that no one treated her with respect, that she was slighted, and so on. But in the last few days she had changed completely. She kept looking at Ilusha’s bed in the corner and seemed lost in thought. She was more silent and quieter, and if she cried, she cried quietly so as not to be heard. The captain saw the change in her with sad bewilderment. At first the boys’ visits only angered her, but later their merry shouts and stories began to divert her. At last she liked them so much that, if the boys had stopped coming, she would have felt dreary without them. When the children told a story or played a game, she laughed and clapped her hands. She called some of them over and kissed them. She was particularly fond of Smurov.

As for the captain, the sight of the children in his room, who came to cheer up Ilusha, filled his heart with rapturous joy from the first. He even hoped that Ilusha would now shake off his low spirits, and that this would hasten his recovery. For all his alarm about Ilusha, until lately he had not felt one minute’s doubt that his boy would get well in the end.

He received his little visitors with reverence and waited on them hand and foot. He was ready to be their horse, and even began letting them ride on his back, but Ilusha did not like the game and it was given up. He began buying little things for them, gingerbread and nuts. He gave them tea and cut sandwiches for them. It must be said that all this time he had plenty of money. He had taken the two hundred roubles from Katerina Ivanovna, just as Alyosha had predicted he would. Later Katerina Ivanovna learned more about their circumstances and Ilusha’s illness, and visited them herself. She got to know the family and managed to charm the half-witted mother. Since then she had helped them generously, and the captain, terror-stricken at the thought that his boy might be dying, forgot his pride and humbly accepted her help.

All this time Doctor Herzenstube, whom Katerina Ivanovna had called in, came punctually every other day, but little was gained by his visits and he dosed the invalid mercilessly. But on that Sunday morning a new doctor was expected, who had come from Moscow, where he had a great reputation. Katerina Ivanovna had sent for him from Moscow at great expense, not specially for Ilusha but for another purpose, of which more will be said in its place later. But since he had come, she had asked him to see Ilusha as well, and the captain had been told to expect him. He had not the slightest idea that Kolya Krassotkin was coming, though he had long wished for a visit from the boy Ilusha was fretting for.

At the moment when Krassotkin opened the door and came into the room, the captain and all the boys were gathered around Ilusha’s bed, looking at a tiny mastiff pup. It had been born only the day before, though the captain had ordered it a week ago to comfort and amuse Ilusha, who was still fretting over the lost and probably dead Zhutchka. Ilusha had heard three days earlier that he was to be given a puppy, and not an ordinary puppy but a pedigree mastiff (a very important point, of course). Out of delicacy he tried to pretend he was pleased. But his father and the boys could not help seeing that the puppy only reminded his little heart of the unhappy dog he had killed. The puppy lay beside him, feebly moving, and he stroked it, smiling sadly, with his thin, pale, wasted hand. Clearly he liked the puppy, but ... it wasn’t Zhutchka. If he could have had Zhutchka and the puppy both, then he would have been completely happy.
“Krassotkin!” one of the boys cried suddenly. He was the first to see him come in.
Krassotkin’s entrance caused a general stir. The boys moved away and stood on each side of the bed, so that he could get a full view of Ilusha. The captain ran eagerly to meet Kolya.
“Please come in ... you’re welcome!” he said hurriedly. “Ilusha, Mr. Krassotkin has come to see you!”

But Krassotkin shook hands with him hurriedly and at once showed that he knew all about the manners of good society. He turned first to the captain’s wife, who was sitting in her armchair, very ill-humored at that moment and grumbling that the boys stood between her and Ilusha’s bed and would not let her see the new puppy. With the greatest courtesy he bowed to her, scraping his foot. Then he turned to Nina and, since she was the only other lady present, made her a similar bow. This polite behavior made an extremely favorable impression on the deranged lady.
“There, you can see right away he’s a young man who’s been well brought up,” she said aloud, throwing up her hands. “But as for our other visitors, they come in one on top of another.”
“What do you mean, mamma, one on top of another? How is that?” the captain muttered affectionately, though a little anxious on her account.
“That’s how they ride in. They get up on each other’s shoulders in the passage and prance in like that on a respectable family. Strange sort of visitors!”
“But who’s come in like that, mamma?”
“Why, that boy came in riding on that one’s back, and this one on that one’s.”

Kolya was already at Ilusha’s bedside. The sick boy turned visibly paler. He raised himself in the bed and looked intently at Kolya. Kolya had not seen his little friend for two months, and the sight of him overwhelmed him. He had never imagined he would see such a wasted, yellow face, such enormous, feverishly glowing eyes and such thin little hands. With grieved surprise he saw Ilusha’s rapid, hard breathing and dry lips. He stepped close, held out his hand and, almost overcome, said:

“Well, old man ... how are you?” But his voice failed him. He couldn’t manage to seem at ease. His face suddenly twitched and the corners of his mouth quivered. Ilusha smiled a pitiful little smile, still unable to say a word. Something moved Kolya to raise his hand and pass it over Ilusha’s hair.
“Never mind!” he murmured softly to him, to cheer him up, or perhaps not knowing why he said it. For a minute they were silent again.
“Hallo, so you’ve got a new puppy?” Kolya said suddenly, in a most callous voice.
“Ye—es,” answered Ilusha in a long whisper, gasping for breath.

“A black nose, that means he’ll be fierce, a good watchdog,” Kolya observed gravely and stolidly, as if the only thing he cared about was the puppy and its black nose. But in reality he still had to do his utmost not to burst out crying like a child, and do what he would, he could not master it. “When he grows up, you’ll have to keep him on a chain, I’m sure.”
“He’ll be a huge dog!” cried one of the boys.
“Of course he will,” “a mastiff,” “large,” “like this,” “as big as a calf,” several voices shouted.

“As big as a calf, a real calf,” chimed in the captain. “I got one like that on purpose, one of the fiercest breed, and his parents are huge and very fierce, they stand this high off the floor.... Sit down here, on Ilusha’s bed, or here on the bench. You’re welcome, we’ve been hoping to see you for a long time.... You were so kind as to come with Alexey Fyodorovitch?”
Krassotkin sat on the edge of the bed, at Ilusha’s feet. He had perhaps prepared a free-and-easy way to open the conversation on the way over, but now he lost the thread of it completely.

“No ... I came with Perezvon. I’ve got a dog now, called Perezvon. It’s a Slavonic name. He’s out there ... if I whistle, he’ll run in. I’ve brought a dog, too,” he said, suddenly addressing Ilusha. “Do you remember Zhutchka, old man?” he suddenly fired the question at him.

Ilusha’s little face quivered. He looked at Kolya with an agonized expression. Alyosha, standing at the door, frowned and signed to Kolya not to speak of Zhutchka, but Kolya did not or would not notice.
